```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(spdep)
library(spatialreg)

#course data (read once for the whole page)
county_covid <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=15njmLhQMvg4KNpFthR0XyS1LD3reotus", quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(2264) |>
  mutate(workplace_drop = -workplace_change)
nc_counties <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1hXVtKL_33c4QRw6_Z9LlYqjgisdYCRqX", quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(2264)

#numbers quoted in the text below come from here, so they stay right if the data changes
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
pv <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", fmt(p, 3))
cov_w_key <- nb2listw(poly2nb(county_covid, queen = TRUE), style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
ols_key <- lm(workplace_drop ~ pct_bachelors, data = county_covid)
lag_key <- lagsarlm(workplace_drop ~ pct_bachelors, data = county_covid, listw = cov_w_key, zero.policy = TRUE)
err_key <- errorsarlm(workplace_drop ~ pct_bachelors, data = county_covid, listw = cov_w_key, zero.policy = TRUE)
```

This tutorial runs over two class days. Day 1 covers ordinary least squares (OLS) regression and checking its residuals for spatial autocorrelation, and Day 2 covers spatial lag and spatial error models. Each day has its own walkthrough, partner practice and index card.

## Day 1 Walkthrough: OLS and Residual Moran's I {#walkthrough}

Run each chunk in your own .Rmd. You will reuse this code in the Day 1 partner practice.

### Step 1: Load the Data and Plot the Relationship

::: {.why}
We'll use `r nrow(county_covid)` North Carolina counties. `pct_bachelors` is the percent of adults with a bachelor's degree, from the [American Community Survey](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs.html), and `workplace_change` is the percent change in visits to workplaces from March to May 2020, from the [Google COVID-19 Community Mobility Reports](https://www.google.com/covid19/mobility/). We flip the sign into `workplace_drop`, so a bigger number means a bigger drop in workplace visits. Our question is whether counties with more college graduates cut back more on going to work in person.
:::

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(spdep)
library(spatialreg)

#county education and mobility, projected to NC State Plane (feet)
county_covid <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=15njmLhQMvg4KNpFthR0XyS1LD3reotus") |>
  st_transform(2264) |>
  mutate(workplace_drop = -workplace_change)
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Scatterplot of the drop in workplace visits against the percent of adults with a bachelor's degree for North Carolina counties, with a fitted line. The points rise from lower left to upper right: counties with more college graduates had larger drops."}
ggplot(county_covid, aes(x = pct_bachelors, y = workplace_drop)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Adults with a bachelor's degree (%)", y = "Drop in workplace visits (%)")
```

### Step 2: Fit the OLS Model

::: {.why}
`lm(y ~ x)` fits the line. The slope says how much y changes for a one-unit change in x, and R-squared is the share of the variation in y that the model explains.
:::

```{r}
ols_model <- lm(workplace_drop ~ pct_bachelors, data = county_covid)
summary(ols_model)
```

Each additional percentage point of college graduates goes with a `r fmt(coef(ols_key)[2])` point larger drop in workplace visits, and R-squared is `r fmt(summary(ols_key)$r.squared)`.

### Step 3: Map the Residuals

::: {.why}
A residual is the observed value minus the model's prediction. If the residuals form patches on the map, the model is missing something spatial and OLS's independence assumption is broken. A diverging palette centered on 0 separates counties the model underpredicts (positive) from counties it overpredicts (negative).
:::

```{r, fig.alt = "Map of OLS residuals by North Carolina county on a diverging scale centered on zero, with a legend. Positive and negative residuals form patches of neighboring counties rather than a random mix."}
county_covid <- county_covid |> mutate(ols_resid = resid(ols_model))

tm_shape(county_covid) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "ols_resid",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "pretty", values = "brewer.rd_bu", midpoint = 0),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "OLS residual"))
```

### Step 4: Test the Residuals with Moran's I

::: {.why}
`lm.morantest()` runs Moran's I on a model's residuals. Use the same neighbors and weights as in the Spatial Autocorrelation tutorial.
:::

```{r}
county_nb <- poly2nb(county_covid, queen = TRUE)
county_w <- nb2listw(county_nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

lm.morantest(ols_model, county_w, zero.policy = TRUE)
```

The residuals' Moran's I is `r fmt(lm.morantest(ols_key, cov_w_key, zero.policy = TRUE)$estimate[1])` (p `r pv(lm.morantest(ols_key, cov_w_key, zero.policy = TRUE)$p.value)`), so the OLS residuals are spatially autocorrelated.

Both partners model `pct_no_health_insur`, the percent of people without health insurance, for North Carolina's 100 counties from the 2019 to 2023 [American Community Survey](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs.html). Partner A uses `pct_pov` (percent in poverty) as the predictor, and Partner B uses `pct_hisp` (percent Hispanic or Latino). Each task tells you in parentheses which walkthrough step to reuse.

```{r, eval = FALSE}

  st_transform(2264)
```

3. Map the residuals. *(Step 3)*
4. Test the residuals with Moran's I, using queen contiguity. *(Step 4)*

## Day 2 Walkthrough: Spatial Lag and Spatial Error Models {#walkthrough-2}

Use the model, neighbors and weights from Day 1.

### Step 1: Choose a Model with the Lagrange Multiplier Tests

::: {.why}
A spatial lag model assumes a county's outcome depends on its neighbors' outcomes. A spatial error model assumes the model's errors are shared with neighbors because of something left out. The Lagrange multiplier tests check for each. If only one of `RSerr` and `RSlag` is significant, use that model. If both are, compare the robust versions, `adjRSerr` and `adjRSlag`, and use the one that is significant or has the smaller p-value.
:::

```{r}
lm.RStests(ols_model, county_w, test = c("RSerr", "RSlag", "adjRSerr", "adjRSlag"),
           zero.policy = TRUE)
```

### Step 2: Spatial Lag Model

::: {.why}
`rho` measures how strongly each county's value depends on its neighbors' values.
:::

```{r}
lag_model <- lagsarlm(workplace_drop ~ pct_bachelors, data = county_covid,
                      listw = county_w, zero.policy = TRUE)
summary(lag_model)
```

### Step 3: Spatial Error Model

::: {.why}
`lambda` measures how strongly the errors are shared between neighbors.
:::

```{r}
error_model <- errorsarlm(workplace_drop ~ pct_bachelors, data = county_covid,
                          listw = county_w, zero.policy = TRUE)
summary(error_model)
```

### Step 4: Compare the Models

::: {.why}
AIC rewards fit and penalizes complexity. A lower AIC is better. Check that the chosen model's residuals are no longer autocorrelated.
:::

```{r}
AIC(ols_model, lag_model, error_model)

#Moran's I on the spatial model's residuals
moran.test(residuals(lag_model), county_w, zero.policy = TRUE)
```

Both simple tests are significant, and only the robust lag test is, so the tests point to a lag model. The lag model also has the lowest AIC (`r fmt(AIC(lag_key), 1)`, compared with `r fmt(AIC(err_key), 1)` for the error model and `r fmt(AIC(ols_key), 1)` for OLS). With rho at `r fmt(lag_key$rho)`, the `pct_bachelors` coefficient falls from `r fmt(coef(ols_key)[2])` to `r fmt(coef(lag_key)["pct_bachelors"])`, because part of what OLS credited to education was really the pull of neighboring counties.

## Answer Key {#answer-key .answer-key}

```{r key-values, include = FALSE}
w_key <- nb2listw(poly2nb(nc_counties, queen = TRUE), style = "W")
fit_all <- function(x) {
  f <- as.formula(paste("pct_no_health_insur ~", x))
  ols <- lm(f, data = nc_counties)
  mt <- lm.morantest(ols, w_key)
  lmt <- lm.RStests(ols, w_key, test = c("RSerr", "RSlag", "adjRSerr", "adjRSlag"))
  lag <- lagsarlm(f, data = nc_counties, listw = w_key)
  err <- errorsarlm(f, data = nc_counties, listw = w_key)
  list(ols = ols, s = summary(ols), mi = mt$estimate[1], mp = mt$p.value, lmt = lmt, lag = lag, err = err,
       err_mi = moran.test(residuals(err), w_key)$estimate[1], err_mp = moran.test(residuals(err), w_key)$p.value)
}
ka <- fit_all("pct_pov")
kb <- fit_all("pct_hisp")
lmp <- function(k, t) pv(k$lmt[[t]]$p.value)
```

### Day 1

| Predictor | Slope | p-value | R-squared | Residual Moran's I | Moran's p-value |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Poverty | `r fmt(coef(ka$ols)[2], 3)` | `r pv(ka$s$coefficients[2, 4])` | `r fmt(ka$s$r.squared)` | `r fmt(ka$mi)` | `r pv(ka$mp)` |
| Hispanic or Latino | `r fmt(coef(kb$ols)[2], 3)` | `r pv(kb$s$coefficients[2, 4])` | `r fmt(kb$s$r.squared)` | `r fmt(kb$mi)` | `r pv(kb$mp)` |

Each additional point of poverty goes with about `r fmt(coef(ka$ols)[2])` more points uninsured, and each additional point of Hispanic or Latino population goes with about `r fmt(coef(kb$ols)[2])` more points uninsured. Both slopes are significant, but both models explain little (poverty more than Hispanic or Latino share). The residuals are clearly autocorrelated in both, so counties next to each other share something about uninsurance that one predictor does not capture.

### Day 2

| Predictor | LM tests choose | OLS coefficient | Error model coefficient | AIC (OLS, lag, error) | Residual Moran's I after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Poverty | Error (adjRSerr p `r lmp(ka, "adjRSerr")`, adjRSlag p `r lmp(ka, "adjRSlag")`) | `r fmt(coef(ka$ols)[2], 3)` | `r fmt(coef(ka$err)["pct_pov"], 3)` | `r fmt(AIC(ka$ols), 1)`, `r fmt(AIC(ka$lag), 1)`, `r fmt(AIC(ka$err), 1)` | `r fmt(ka$err_mi)` (p `r pv(ka$err_mp)`) |
| Hispanic or Latino | Error (adjRSerr p `r lmp(kb, "adjRSerr")`, adjRSlag p `r lmp(kb, "adjRSlag")`) | `r fmt(coef(kb$ols)[2], 3)` | `r fmt(coef(kb$err)["pct_hisp"], 3)` | `r fmt(AIC(kb$ols), 1)`, `r fmt(AIC(kb$lag), 1)`, `r fmt(AIC(kb$err), 1)` | `r fmt(kb$err_mi)` (p `r pv(kb$err_mp)`) |

Lambda is `r fmt(ka$err$lambda)` for Partner A and `r fmt(kb$err$lambda)` for Partner B. A good card says something like this. For both predictors the tests point to a spatial error model, which means uninsurance clusters because of things the model leaves out that are shared by neighboring counties, such as regional job markets, the mix of employers that offer insurance, or distance to health care, rather than because one county's uninsurance spreads to the next. After the error model, the residuals are no longer significantly autocorrelated.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
nc_counties <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1hXVtKL_33c4QRw6_Z9LlYqjgisdYCRqX") |>
  st_transform(2264)

county_nb <- poly2nb(nc_counties, queen = TRUE)
county_w <- nb2listw(county_nb, style = "W")

#### Partner A: poverty (swap in pct_hisp for Partner B) ####

#Day 1
ggplot(nc_counties, aes(x = pct_pov, y = pct_no_health_insur)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black") +
  labs(x = "People in poverty (%)", y = "People without health insurance (%)")

ols_a <- lm(pct_no_health_insur ~ pct_pov, data = nc_counties)
summary(ols_a)

nc_counties <- nc_counties |> mutate(resid_a = resid(ols_a))
tm_shape(nc_counties) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "resid_a",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "pretty", values = "brewer.rd_bu", midpoint = 0),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "OLS residual"))

lm.morantest(ols_a, county_w)

#Day 2
lm.RStests(ols_a, county_w, test = c("RSerr", "RSlag", "adjRSerr", "adjRSlag"))

lag_a <- lagsarlm(pct_no_health_insur ~ pct_pov, data = nc_counties, listw = county_w)
summary(lag_a)

error_a <- errorsarlm(pct_no_health_insur ~ pct_pov, data = nc_counties, listw = county_w)
summary(error_a)

AIC(ols_a, lag_a, error_a)
moran.test(residuals(error_a), county_w)
```
